architect: Engineer Alberto Robles Gil (works director); iron structure imported from Belgium, contracted with Óscar Braniff; foundations by Eduardo Sabathe
lost: 1946: last corrida 19 May 1946; sold that year for dismantling (7 million pesos) and moved in its entirety to Cuatro Caminos
now: El Palacio de Hierro department store, southeast corner of Durango and Salamanca

items.en:
One of the buildings now gone that stood out on its own merits was the famous Toreo de la Condesa (1907–1946), where brilliant pages of Mexican bullfighting were written. To carry out this project, which aspired to be the finest bullring in the world, a public limited company was formed under the name Nueva Empresa de El Toreo S.A., with a capital of 500,000 pesos and a board of directors made up of the following people: Manuel Fernández del Castillo y de Mier, president, of whom don Alfonso de Icaza, recalling this bullring, said: “it was made by a rich man who died poor”; Lucas Alamán, Miguel Illanes and the engineer José Mondragón, members; Emilio Rodríguez, treasurer; Carlos Cuesta, commissioner; the lawyer Roberto A. Esteva Ruiz, secretary; and finally José del Rivero, manager.
The bullring was built on block number 48 of what was originally the colonia Condesa, from which it took its name. It had an area of 18,425 square metres and a location that offered great advantages, since it could be seen from all four sides and the public could thus recognize it immediately.
The engineer Alberto Robles Gil directed the works, whose main features were: a structure made entirely of iron and steel; cement flooring in the lumbreras (upper boxes) and the tendido (tiered seating); a ring 45 metres in diameter; and a callejón (passageway around the ring) two metres wide. There were three rows of barrera seats with their own entrances and 16 rows of tendido seating divided by a walkway. Other walkways divided the tendidos into upper and lower sections, with various entrances that allowed easy access. From the last step of the tendido, at a height of about two metres, began a series of open boxes of four seats each; behind these were another four rows of tendido seating and two tiers of lumbreras.
Everything relating to the iron structure, imported from Belgium, was contracted with Óscar Braniff, who undertook to deliver it finished on 20 October 1907; otherwise he was to pay a penalty of a thousand pesos for each day of delay. Fortunately for him, the bullring was completed before the deadline. The foundation works, which consisted of a grillage of iron, concrete and masonry, were carried out by don Eduardo Sabathe, who handed them over three days before the agreed date. The bullring held 23,000 spectators, and its total cost, including the land, was 600,000 pesos.
As additional details, it may be mentioned that in its early days admission to the novilladas cost no more than one peso in the shaded section and 25 centavos in the sunny section. Moreover, bulls from the Santín, Piedras Negras and Tepeyahualco ranches had already been secured for the first corridas, as well as the appearance of Antonio Fuentes, “the Bullfighter of Elegance.”
El Toreo was inaugurated on 22 September 1907 with the following bill: Manuel González Rerre and Agustín Velasco Bombita, Spanish and Mexican respectively, fighting four bulls from the Tepeyahualco ranch, together with another four young bulls of the same brand for the young novilleros Samuel Solís and Pascual Bueno. The first bull to enter this ring was named Barrilito, and admission prices were: four-seat boxes, 20 pesos; front-row barrera, 8 pesos, and in the sun 3 pesos; general admission, shade 4 pesos and sun 1.50. Not all aficionados, however, welcomed the new bullring, as don Alfonso de Icaza notes: “when it opened it was branded as not very taurine, as cold, as looking more like a Texas stadium than a bullring...”
Many important events took place in this ring, such as the celebration of the centenary of the consummation of Independence (1821–1921), held on Sunday 11 September with a bill unbeatable in its day: Rodolfo Gaona, Ignacio Sánchez Mejías and Juan Silvetti. There are also records of performances by internationally famous singers such as Tita Rufo, Fleta and the celebrated Italian tenor Enrico Caruso, who appeared in 1919.
An anecdote worth remembering took place in this bullring when General Álvaro Obregón had as a guest in his front-row barrera seat the Spanish writer Ramón del Valle-Inclán. As is well known, the general had lost his right arm in battle and the writer lacked his left hand, so the latter, in a spontaneous gesture, proposed to Obregón: “Lend me your left hand, Mr. President, so I can applaud!”
Finally, we shall mention some of the many bullfighters who left proof of their art and courage in the ring of this plaza: Rodolfo Gaona, el Califa de León; Vicente Segura; Juan Belmonte, el Fenómeno de Triana; José Moreno, Lagartijillo chico; Luis Freg, don Valor; Ignacio Sánchez Mejías; Vicente Pastor, el Chico de la blusa; Juan Silvetti, el Tigre de Guanajuato; Manuel Jiménez, Chicuelo; Marcial Lalanda; Pepe Ortiz; Antonio Márquez; Rafael González, Machaquito; Domingo González, Dominguín; Carmelo Pérez, who died as a result of a goring received in this ring; José González, Carnicerito de México; Fermín Espinoza, Armillita; Jesús Solórzano; Alberto Balderas, el Torero de México, who died in this ring on 29 December 1940 from a goring by the bull Cobijero of the Piedras Negras ranch, which had originally been drawn for Carnicerito; Lorenzo Garza, el Ave de las tempestades; Luis Castro, el Soldado; Silverio Pérez, el Faraón de Texcoco; Ricardo Torres, Bombita chico; Fermín Rivera; Rafael Gómez, el Gallo; Joaquín Rodríguez, Cagancho; Francisco Vega de los Reyes, Gitanillo de Triana; Pepe Luis Vázquez; Juan Luis de la Rosa; Manuel Rodríguez, Manolete; Andrés Blando; Carlos Arruza, el Ciclón; Alfonso Ramírez, el Calesero; Miguel Báez, Litri.
With so many great figures of the fiesta brava, it can be said that this bullring filled one of the most brilliant eras of the bullfighting art in our country. The last corrida at the Toreo de la Condesa took place on Sunday 19 May 1946, with a bill as lacklustre as that of its inauguration: Andrés Blando, Edmundo Cepeda and the Colombian Miguel López, fighting three bulls from Atenco and as many again from the San Diego de los Padres ranch. That same year the bullring was sold for dismantling for seven million pesos and moved in its entirety to Cuatro Caminos. Its site is now occupied by the El Palacio de Hierro department store, at the southeast corner of Durango and Salamanca streets.

lost: Demolished (date not given); replaced by the Archdiocese building
now: Twelve-storey building of the Archdiocese of Mexico (la Mitra), Durango 90; damaged in 1985 and quickly and completely restored

items.en: A few metres away, at Durango 90 on the corner of Córdoba, the twelve-storey building of the Archdiocese of Mexico rises like a modern Tower of Babel. On that site stood a lovely Porfirian residence that did not clash with its neighbour, the Castillo de las Brujas.

[After the 1985 earthquake...] there were also damaged buildings that went through a slow process of restoration [...]. By contrast, the modern building of the Mitra [Archdiocese], at Durango 90, was restored completely and quickly.
At Orizaba 43, on the corner of the plaza Río de Janeiro, stood a large residence surrounded by a beautiful garden; in its place two utterly nondescript buildings were put up. [...]

lost: Main house demolished (date not given); only the brick stables and servants' quarters with mansards survive
now: A plain commercial building (billiard hall and restaurant); the surviving stables and servants' quarters

items.en: At Jalapa 12 stood the residence of the last ambassador of the Austro-Hungarian Empire; all that remains of it are the stables and the servants' quarters, built of brick and topped with mansards, which are enough to give an idea of the former majesty of the main house. Its site is now occupied by a plain commercial building (a billiard hall and restaurant), and it is a real pity that no photograph of it exists.

lost: Survived until “a few years ago” (relative to the book); demolished for the Plaza Córdoba building
now: The Plaza Córdoba building: eleven floors of offices and three of parking

items.en: [...] The chalet built by the Lamm engineers, which survived until a few years ago at Córdoba 42, was surrounded by an enormous garden. Such a generous plot was the deciding factor in building in its place the enormous Plaza Córdoba building, which, with its eleven floors of offices and three of parking, breaks brutally with the original character of this street.

now: A parking lot, almost opposite the Sagrada Familia church

items.en: Doña Socorro Pous de Moheno, who settled in the colonia around 1920, recalls: “[...] Don Leopoldo Gout’s house was so beautiful that people would stop to admire it; it stood on what is now a parking lot, almost opposite the Sagrada Familia. I used to visit it, and I remember that the floors of its bathrooms were of English porcelain... [...]”

lost: Both demolished (dates not given): the first for the court tower; the second, “until recently” standing, for a parking lot
now: First house (Robles Gil family): glass tower housing the Tribunal Superior de Justicia del Distrito Federal and the family courts; second house: a parking lot

items.en: Another example of destruction is the pair of residences that stood on the corner of avenida Insurgentes and Colima. The first belonged to the Robles Gil family, and in its place an enormous glass tower was built that houses the Tribunal Superior de Justicia del Distrito Federal (the Federal District's High Court of Justice) and the family courts. Until recently another fine example of a Porfirian mansion could be seen beside it; it was destroyed to make a parking lot.

lost: Earthquake of 19 September 1985: Córdoba 86 had to be demolished after several walls of the adjoining building fell on it; Córdoba 82-82bis was left with deep cracks (still visible) and immediately evacuated

items.en: Walking through the Roma a few days after the earthquake and looking at the exteriors of the buildings from the first three decades of the twentieth century, we were able to see that only three houses had been totally destroyed and two more partially: the building at Córdoba 82-82bis showed deep cracks (they can still be seen) that led to its immediate evacuation; the one at Córdoba 86 had to be demolished, since several walls of the adjoining building fell on it; [...] In many other old buildings, existing cracks grew worse; official figures record a total of 197 damaged dwellings and 946 injured residents in this colonia.

General Álvaro Obregón lived in the house (since demolished) at number 185 of the avenue that was then still called Jalisco. Curiously, at number 187 of the same avenue lived, after her return from the Islas Marías, Concepción Acevedo de la Llata, better known as Madre Conchita, who was accused of having been an accomplice and the mastermind of the assassination of General Obregón carried out by José de León Toral.

architect: Built for/by the rich Spaniard Eusebio González, “el Burro de Oro” (per Socorro Pous de Moheno's memoir)
now: The 1946 three-storey apartment building with large shops on the ground floor

items.en: On the southwest corner of Álvaro Obregón and Orizaba, a beautiful mansion could be admired until the mid-1940s. The imagination of the person who tore it down stretched only as far as building, in 1946, the insipid building of three floors of apartments and large shops that broke the architectural harmony kept until then by the buildings on the four corners of that intersection.

Doña Socorro Pous de Moheno, who settled in the colonia around 1920, recalls: “[...] As for the most beautiful houses of that time, I remember the one at Obregón and Orizaba built by the rich Spaniard Eusebio González, whom they nicknamed ‘el Burro de Oro’ [the Golden Donkey], who knows why. [...]”

lost: Earthquake of 19 September 1985: already in ruinous condition, it destroyed its neighbour Chiapas 61a (the text does not state its own fate explicitly)

items.en: Walking through the Roma a few days after the earthquake and looking at the exteriors of the buildings from the first three decades of the twentieth century, we were able to see that only three houses had been totally destroyed and two more partially: [...] the one at Chiapas 61a was completely destroyed by its neighbour, Chihuahua 72, which had been in a ruinous state for a long time [...]. In many other old buildings, existing cracks grew worse; official figures record a total of 197 damaged dwellings and 946 injured residents in this colonia.

[...] The baker of the Tel-Aviv bakery, which was on the ground floor of the building at Guanajuato 50-52-54, used to remark that “it was in the cine Royal [since demolished], which stood right here on the corner of Mérida and Guanajuato, that the cry of ‘¡cácaro!’ was heard for the first time in Mexico.”
Of the Roma's three cinemas, the Royal, the Roma and the Balmori, all now gone, the last stood out; on its premiere nights great searchlights and orchestral music were used. [...]

lost: Earthquake of 19 September 1985: destroyed by the effect of its neighbour

items.en: Walking through the Roma a few days after the earthquake and looking at the exteriors of the buildings from the first three decades of the twentieth century, we were able to see that only three houses had been totally destroyed and two more partially: [...] and the one at Querétaro 171 was also destroyed by the effect of its neighbour. In many other old buildings, existing cracks grew worse; official figures record a total of 197 damaged dwellings and 946 injured residents in this colonia.

lost: Earthquake of 19 September 1985: completely destroyed by its neighbour, Chihuahua 72, which had long been in ruins
